Pentagon waters down Trump’s European troop drawdown plans
 
The Trump administration’s ambitious plans to pull out 25k-35k of the ~80k troops the US has stationed in Europe has been pared down to the bone, sources familiar with deliberations told Bloomberg.
Allies now expect an overall pullback of just ~5k troops - 1/5 or less of the initial estimate.
It won’t be the first time the Pentagon or State Department have gone back on a Trump pledge for a troop drawdown.
In late 2020, after Trump lost his first bid for reelection, then-special representative for Syria James Jeffrey boasted that he and his team had played “shell games” with the president on the number of troops in Syria, and ignored withdrawal orders. US forces ultimately remained in the country until April 2026, long after Bashar Assad fled and a new, al-Qaeda-linked president was installed.
This week, Romania proposed that European countries [pay the US to keep and expand its troop presence](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77665) along NATO’s eastern flank with Russia.

🇮🇷 Iran war will end up costing US $1 TRILLION, former White House economist says
 
🔊“They’re almost approaching $50B in expenditures – so the transparent things that Hegseth’s been forced to say – it’s close to $50B. I have estimated at the end of the day, this thing will cost a trillion dollars,” Johns Hopkins economics professor Steve Hanke told the [Wealthion podcast](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77309).
Hanke, who served as a senior member of the Council of Economic Advisors in the first years of the Reagan administration, when it was trying to tackle the stagflationary crisis of the early 80s, bases his estimate on historical precedent, including the second Bush administration’s guesstimate that the Iraq War would cost $200B, vs an actual final cost of up to $5T (25 times higher).
🗣“Applying that same multiple to the current conflict, if the war winds down quickly, the final direct cost for the war on Iran will likely reach at least $1 trillion,” Hanke says.
Hanke isn’t alone. Harvard Kennedy School lecturer Linda Bilmes, who previously accurately predicted that the Iraq War would cost trillions, estimated the Iran war’s price tag would reach $1T or more. University of Michigan economist Johnathan Wolfers said in May that military costs plus energy prices, inflation, interest rate hikes and slowed growth would cost from $400B to “very possibly trillions.”
Others predict even more extreme consequences, up to and including a housing, stock or bond market crisis, or a collapse of the dollar triggered by a vicious circle of energy price hikes, inflation, higher interest rates and higher government [borrowing costs](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75711).

🇮🇱🚀 Israeli troops crash West Bank wedding, abduct groom and attack guests using tear gas
 
A large wedding ceremony attended by ~150 people in the central West Bank village of al-Mughayyir was broken up by armed Israeli troops on Friday night, with soldiers arresting the groom and three guests and holding them for several hours before letting them go.
Troops fired tear gas into the reception hall, and closed the main entrance to the village. Amateur footage showed a spent tear gas cannister and empty tables and chairs, some overturned, alongside plates and food strewn over the floor at the venue site.
 
The wedding raid was one of several similar operations by the IDF in the West Bank over the past 24 hours:
➡️ on Friday, IDF patrols attacked a welcoming ceremony for a freed Palestinian detainee in the Jericho and Jordan Valley area, dispersing attendees and damaging the venue
➡️ on Saturday, troops arrested 10 people in Nablus and two nearby refugee camps, beating up several young men and seizing a home, evicting its residents and setting up a base of operations
➡️ raids, searches and tightened checkpoint restrictions were also reported in Tammun, the Wadi Burqin area outside Jenin and a refugee camp outside Hebron
 
The crackdown comes amid what has become the most violent year for Palestinian West Bank [residents](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77394) since recording began, with the UN reporting 2.1k+ settler attacks on area villages and farms, seizures of property and livestock, [sabotage and deadly beatings](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76606).
Mandated to stop settler violence, the IDF has often instead sided with them, while top Israeli officials have threatened a ‘Gaza and Lebanon-style’ operation in the West Bank.

A recent investigation by The Cradle reveals how the UAE has built a transnational recruitment network that moves Colombian veterans into Sudan to fight alongside the Rapid Support Forces, the paramilitary group accused of genocide in Darfur.
🔴 A confidential UN report submitted to the Security Council in November 2026 found that an Emirati security company, Global Security Services Group, with close ties to the government, moved the Colombians through territory controlled by Emirati proxies in Libya and Somalia
🔴 The recruits were told they were taking security jobs. A decent part, however, ended up on the front lines operating drones, artillery, and military vehicles, and some trained RSF fighters, including children

Investigators estimated that as many as 2,000 former Colombian military personnel were recruited through these [networks](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/54772). Most of them transited through the UAE without border checks and official registration, indicating state backing.
The ownership trail also leads into the Emirati political establishment. The recruiting company's founder, Ahmed Mohammed al-Humairi, served as secretary-general of the UAE Presidential Court.
The Sudan operation is a continuation of a long history of the UAE using foreign military contractors.
🔶 The UAE used mercenaries in Yemen and Libya. In Libya, companies linked to Prince participated in Project Opus (2019), supporting Haftar's forces with foreign fighters, attack helicopters, drones, and intelligence
🔶 In Ethiopia, with UAE support, a military camp for 10,000 people was opened, where RSF fighters undergo [military training ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/64367)
Specifically in Sudan, the UAE is interested in gaining access to Sudan's Red Sea port to control an important trade artery, as well as access to vast gold reserves controlled by the anti-government RSF forces. In addition, the UAE is countering [the influence of Turkey](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/53600) and Saudi Arabia, which are helping the government in Khartoum.
At the same time, the UAE is trying to silence its critics on all fronts. Both [the ICC](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71593) and [the UK](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71320) face their own corruption allegations and accusations of ignoring UAE crimes. events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🔍👁️ Tech firm that deployed AI dashboard into FAA systems days before outage insists it’s not to blame
 
🔊“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of Air Space Intelligence or our integration with the Federal Aviation Administration and Air Traffic Control,” the company tweeted after the FAA issued a four-hour nationwide grounding of all flights on Friday, citing a “temporary [telecommunications outage.”](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77743)
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “old legacy equipment” for the stoppage and asked for $50B to [fix the problem](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77746).
The timing of the stop – three days after SMART was introduced across all 22 US Air Route Traffic Control Centers on November 10, has raised red flags.
In October, federal lawmakers asked the Government Accountability Office to conduct an independent review of the new AI system, expressing concerns about a potential lack of input from controllers, and insufficient safety testing.
Sean Duffy insisted Friday that the new equipment was not to blame, saying “SMART is completely disconnected [and] not even plugged in.”
SMART, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, is a cloud-based software package providing a predictive planning layer for controllers, synthesizing data pulled from ~200 data streams on factors like weather, flight schedules, runway capacity and controller staffing into a single dashboard.
The government assures human beings are left in charge of actual air traffic control functions. But the system’s reliance on external network connections has raised concerns about the potential to feed it distorted or ‘poisoned’ data to adversely impact human decision-making.
